chunks: "A sense resistor works by Ohm's law. I put a small, precise resistor in series with the load, so the full load current flows through it.
The voltage across it is V equals I times R sense . I know R sense , so measuring that voltage tells me the current.
The resistor needs to be small, a few milliohms to maybe a few hundred, so it doesn't steal much voltage or burn much power: at 5 amps and 10 milliohms I get 50 millivolts and a quarter of a watt.

That millivolt signal is tiny and often sits on a large common-mode voltage if it's on the high side, so I use a current sense amplifier to amplify the difference and shift it to a ground-referenced range, and then an ADC reads it.
Firmware divides back by gain and resistance to get amps.

Two practical details: I connect the sense wires directly to the resistor pads, Kelvin style, so trace resistance isn't part of the measurement, and I make sure the resistor's power rating and tolerance fit the application."
